revisions.title: Two legal postures at the King Archon's court
revisions.body: The opening brings Socrates and Euthyphro together at the King Archon's court, but it does not yet tell us what Euthyphro's case concerns. Socrates' case is identified as a public indictment, and Meletus' reported charge concerns making new gods and rejecting the old ones. Only at the end of the span does the dialogue clarify their opposite postures: Socrates is being prosecuted, while Euthyphro is prosecuting.

Socrates turns Meletus' accusation into a generous picture of civic reform. The young are to be tended first, like young plants, and the elders afterward; the legal charge is thus recast as a program for cultivating the city. Because this sequence is Socrates' report, and because he presents Meletus' wisdom and future benefits with hedging, the praise sounds less like a settled account than a pointedly charitable reconstruction.

Euthyphro groups himself with Socrates as a target of public mockery, but Socrates' reply shifts the issue from ridicule to teaching. Socrates suggests—not establishes—that Euthyphro may seem reserved while he himself may seem to distribute his wisdom freely. The contrast is therefore a conjecture within the exchange, and its force lies in the different public dangers it imagines: unusual cleverness versus making others like oneself.

Euthyphro’s account makes the charge morally difficult without settling the facts for us. He narrates that a hired laborer killed a household slave in a drunken rage; his father then bound the man, sent for religious instructions, and neglected him until he died. But this remains Euthyphro’s own, independently unverified account. The details therefore complicate his prosecution rather than prove it. Listen for how confidently he builds a religious judgment on a story whose facts have not been established beyond his telling.

Euthyphro does offer a definition—but it is a definition by example. He identifies piety with the prosecution he is carrying out, even when the offender is a relative. That makes the answer vivid and morally forceful, but it still names one kind of action rather than the feature shared by pious actions generally. The point is not that the prosecution cannot be pious; it is that an example does not yet supply the form by which other cases can be judged.

Here Socrates tests Euthyphro’s definition against Euthyphro’s own concessions. If the gods disagree about justice and goodness, one god may love what another hates; and if holiness means what the gods love, the same things receive opposite classifications within that definition. The point is not to settle whether the gods truly agree, or to state Plato’s theology. It is a conditional refutation: Euthyphro’s definition cannot remain intact alongside his claim that the gods disagree.

At 9c, Socrates does not show that Euthyphro’s promised proof cannot be given. He brackets it: even if Euthyphro proved that every god condemns the laborer’s death, Socrates still would not have learned what holiness is, because the proposed god-hated marker has already appeared as god-loved too. The proof would establish only the status of this act, not supply a definition. Socrates therefore redirects the inquiry and proposes a unanimity formula—what all gods hate is unholy, what all love holy—leaving it for Euthyphro to accept and examine.

revisions.title: The direction of explanation
revisions.body: Socrates turns Euthyphro's revised definition into a test of explanatory direction. The pious is loved because it is pious, while the god-loved is god-loved because it is loved; Socrates therefore treats them as different. The phrase "loved by all the gods" supplies a property of the pious, not its essence. The argument rejects the definition by showing that its explanation points in the wrong direction.

Socrates opens with the dilemma: is the holy loved because it is holy, or holy because it is loved? Euthyphro replies that he does not know what Socrates means. Socrates responds by separating active and passive expressions—carrying from being carried, seeing from being seen—and then asks whether loving differs from being loved. A careful reading should hear this as clarification in progress, not proof that Euthyphro lacks the distinction.

Socrates now names the kind of answer he thinks Euthyphro has supplied: a pathos, something that happens to the holy—being loved by all the gods—in place of making its ousia clear. That distinction shifts the question from what accompanies the holy to what the holy is. The passage sends Euthyphro back to the definition; it does not establish that he has no answer to give.

revisions.title: From instability to structure
revisions.body: At 11b the discussion reaches a comic impasse: Euthyphro's proposed account will not stay put, and Socrates answers with a Daedalus comparison. The ancestry reference belongs to the joke, not to a settled claim about lineage; the immediate point is that the statements are Euthyphro's. The inquiry then resets: piety is treated as a part of justice, and Euthyphro identifies that part with care of the gods.

Here the Daedalus image makes argumentative instability visible. Euthyphro says that whatever they propose keeps moving; Socrates compares the statements to Daedalus's works, then points out that the hypotheses are Euthyphro's. Socrates finally calls himself clever against his will, claiming that his questioning can make other people's arguments move as well as his own. The joke thus turns a technical difficulty into a comic negotiation of responsibility: the dialogue leaves the instability shared, rather than assigning it straightforwardly to one speaker.

revisions.title: Exchange, honor, and the return to god-loved
revisions.body: Euthyphro’s ritual account shifts the discussion toward exchange: prayer asks, sacrifice gives, and Socrates tests what the gods receive. Euthyphro answers with honor and gratitude, then agrees that piety is what is dear to the gods. The return is the point: it reopens the earlier distinction between pious and god-loved, so the definition has not advanced—not because the record settles a final refutation, but because the conversation has reached an unresolved inconsistency.
